title: Larger shallow earthquakes had fewer, not more, earlier M 4.5-4.9 events within 50 km in global ComCat data for 1990-2026; ETAS null catalogs gave no such decrease
abstract: Question: does the number of small earthquakes before an earthquake increase with its magnitude? Standard ETAS models predict no dependence. A preparation model predicts a positive dependence. Approach: we used the USGS ComCat global catalog (M 4.5 or more, 1973-2026). Targets were shallow (70 km or less) events of M 5.0 or more in 1990-2026 with no M 5 or more event within 100 km in the 30 days before (26,258 targets). For each target, we counted M 4.5-4.9 events within 50 km in the 30 days before. A conditional Poisson model with 5 degree cell x era strata and a 5-year background term gave the change in log count per magnitude unit (beta). We wrote the plan before we computed outcomes. We applied the same code to 48 synthetic global ETAS catalogs (four variants, including short-term incompleteness). Result: beta = -0.175 (stratum bootstrap 95% interval -0.267 to -0.080; permutation p = 0.001). Larger targets had fewer earlier small events: the rate ratio for M 7 against M 5 was 0.70 (0.59-0.85). The ETAS catalogs gave beta from -0.080 to +0.063 (mean -0.01). The decrease was largest within 25 km (-0.34) and in the last day (-0.33). It was absent at 25-50 km and 100-200 km. Thus we find no growth of the foreshock area with magnitude. Targets after local activity had a higher b-value (1.11 against 1.01). Post-hoc checks (1 degree strata, local history covariates, volcano exclusion, an incompleteness guard) changed beta little. The value was smaller for free-depth targets (-0.086, SE 0.054) and Mw-type targets (-0.12, SE 0.05). Limitations: mixed magnitude types (mb and Mw), M 4.5 completeness that changes in space and time, epicentre-based distances, and a simple ETAS null. We cannot separate a physical cause (for example higher b-values in bursts) from catalog effects. The study does not cover foreshocks of M 5 or more.

Felzer et al. (2004) found no dependence of foreshock number on mainshock magnitude in global data; we also find no positive dependence, but we find a negative one.
Lippiello et al. (2012) reported foreshock numbers and spatial organization that depend on mainshock magnitude; our global test finds a decrease with magnitude and no growth of foreshock extent.
